item.title: Nankinmachi: Kobe's Chinatown — Guide
item.description: Nankinmachi, Kobe’s Chinatown, is one of only three in Japan and grew from the Chinese merchant community that settled here after the port opened to foreign trade in 1868. Compact and lively, it centres on a small square with an ornate pavilion, entered through vivid red-and-gold gates and lined with lanterns overhead. The real draw is the street food: stalls and shopfronts sell steaming buta-man pork buns, dumplings, fried noodles, sweet sesame balls and roast duck, and the pleasure is simply to graze your way through the lanes with something hot in each hand.

item.title: Yokohama Chinatown Cooking Guide: Classes, Tips & Access
item.description: Japan’s biggest Chinatown, in Yokohama, isn’t just for eating — it’s a great place to learn to cook the very dishes that make it famous. Amid the lantern-hung streets and hundreds of restaurants, cooking studios and classes let visitors get hands-on, folding their own dumplings, shumai and steamed buns, or rolling dim sum under a chef’s guidance, before sitting down to eat what they made. It’s a fun, interactive way to dive deeper into Chinatown than a meal alone, take home a new skill, and understand the Cantonese and regional Chinese cuisine that has thrived in Yokohama since the port opened in the 19th century.

item.title: Yokohama Chinatown Guide: Food, Gates & Access
item.description: Yokohama Chinatown (Chukagai) is the largest Chinatown in Japan — and one of the biggest in the world — a vibrant, lantern-strung warren of some 600 shops and restaurants packed into a few colourful blocks. Marked by ornate paifang gates in every direction, it’s a feast for the senses: steaming dim sum, sizzling street snacks, ornate temples and shops bursting with sweets and souvenirs. Born from Yokohama’s opening as a port in 1859, it’s both a culinary destination and a lively cultural quarter, and an essential stop on any Yokohama visit.
